title: Chapter 5 — Your Personal Operating System
intro: A sales job without structure is just showing up and hoping. This chapter gives you the daily and weekly system that turns a job into a business.

sections.title: Treat Your Career Like a Business
sections.content:
The top salespeople on every floor do not think of themselves as employees. They think of themselves as business owners who happen to work inside someone else's building.

They manage their own pipeline. They track their own numbers. They invest in their own development. They build their own client relationships. They control what they can control.

That mindset changes everything — because when you think like a business owner, downtime becomes an investment opportunity, not a break.

sections.title: The Daily System
sections.content:
Before customers arrive, the best salespeople have already started working.

Morning: walk the floor, check displays, note inventory gaps, review today's deliveries and pending quotes. Check CRM for follow-ups due today. Review any new products or promotions.

During the day: follow the 10 Steps with every customer. Between customers — follow up on open quotes, call past customers, update CRM records, study product information.

End of day: log every customer interaction. Update notes on pending deals. Set tomorrow's follow-up priorities. Review what went well and what you would do differently.

This takes discipline. Most people will not do it. That is exactly why it works — because the people who do it consistently outperform everyone who does not.

sections.title: The Weekly Review
sections.content:
Once a week, sit down and look at your numbers honestly.

How many customers did I work this week? What was my closing percentage? How many follow-ups did I make? How many quotes are still open? What is in my pipeline for next week? What skills do I need to work on?

This is not about beating yourself up. It is about catching problems early and making adjustments before a bad week becomes a bad month.

The salespeople who review their numbers weekly almost always outperform those who only look at their numbers when a manager forces them to.

sections.title: Your CRM Is Your Business Plan
sections.content:
Your CRM is not a task your manager makes you do. It is your business plan.

Every customer you log is a future opportunity. Every follow-up you schedule is a potential sale. Every note you add is context that makes the next conversation more personal and more effective.

The salesperson with a clean, active CRM has a business. The salesperson with an empty CRM has a hope. There is a meaningful difference between those two things.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating personal operating systems, ask:

Does the salesperson have a daily routine — or do they wing it?
Do they use downtime productively?
Do they review their own numbers weekly?
Is their CRM active and current — or dusty and ignored?
Do they treat their role like a business — or just a job?

The structure is simple. The discipline to maintain it is what separates careers.
